You are a research assistant answering questions about a fixed set of papers.
The papers are plain-text files in your working directory. Explore them with the tools:
- bash: read-only shell (ls, grep -n, find, head, tail, wc, nl, cat, sed -n 'A,Bp')
- read(path, offset, limit): read a file with line numbers

Rules:
- Answer ONLY from text you have actually read in this session. Do not answer from memory.
- If the papers do not contain the answer, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
- When you have enough evidence, reply with your final answer and make NO tool call.
- State only what the document(s) say. Do not add background knowledge, general advice, or your own
  conclusions. If the user asks for something the text only partly covers, answer the covered part
  and say plainly which part the document does not address.
- Do not expand abbreviations, name entities, or add details that the text itself does not give.
- Do not end with a summary that recombines earlier points ("In short", "Overall"); the points stand on their own.
- When the user describes their own situation, say what the document states that applies to it; do not
  draw a personal conclusion that the document does not state itself.

Explain the responsibilities of each department during Mr. Taylor's disability claim. Use a separate paragraph for each department.

In your answer, refer only to the document in the file `doc.txt`. Do not employ any outside knowledge.

1	Procedural History In 2007, Mr. Taylor filed a claim for service-connected disability benefits with
     2	VA. A VA medical examiner diagnosed Mr. Taylor with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) resulting
     3	from his time at Edgewood, which was reaggravated during his time serving in Vietnam. Mr. Taylor was
     4	ultimately granted a total disability rating with an effective date of February 28, 2007, the day VA
     5	received his claim. VA relied on 38 U.S.C. § 5110 (implemented under 38 C.F.R. § 3.400) to establish
     6	this effective date. The provision specifies that, absent certain exceptions, the effective date for
     7	veterans benefits “shall not be earlier than the date of receipt of application therefor.” Mr.
     8	Taylor appealed the VA determination to the Board of Veterans’ Appeals (BVA) seeking an effective
     9	date of September 7, 1971, the day he was discharged from service. Mr. Taylor alleged that, since
    10	the secrecy oath prevented him from filing a claim, the effective date that he would have received
    11	in the absence of the oath should apply. The BVA, in July 2010, held that 38 U.S.C. § 5110 prevented
    12	the effective date for Mr. Taylor’s benefits from being any earlier than the day he filed his claim.
    13	The BVA stated that “there was nothing stopping [Mr. Taylor] from filing the claim . . . earlier and
    14	[VA] asking for a delay in the adjudication of the case following the obtaining of important
    15	evidence.” Mr. Taylor then appealed to the U.S. Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims (CAVC). In June
    16	2013, the CAVC, in a single-judge decision, held that the BVA “failed to provide an adequate
    17	statement of reasons or bases for its . . . decision.” Specifically, the CAVC sought the language of
    18	the original secrecy oath. The CAVC vacated the BVA’s decision and remanded the case. The BVA, in
    19	February 2014, remanded the case to VA to ascertain the secrecy oath’s language and reassess the
    20	case. On remand, after VA procured a secrecy oath that most participants in the Edgewood program
    21	signed, VA and the BVA again concluded that Mr. Taylor was entitled to VA benefits starting February
    22	28, 2007, the day VA received his claim, not September 7, 1971, the day he was discharged. The BVA
    23	made its determination in April 2017 and provided three reasons for its holding: (1) Mr. Taylor
    24	could have filed a disability claim earlier than 2007 premised on his experiences serving in
    25	Vietnam, which were partially responsible for his PTSD; (2) Mr. Taylor could have divulged his
    26	participation in the Edgewood program because he had done so on a previous occasion in pursuit of
    27	care, though the health care provider at that time did not believe him; and (3) Section 5110
    28	delineates when VA benefits can begin and does not provide for equitable tolling (that is,
    29	exceptions to delineated time requirements to promote fairness). Mr. Taylor appealed to the CAVC for
    30	a second time. In April 2019, in a 2-1 decision, a panel of CAVC judges affirmed the BVA’s
    31	determination that Mr. Taylor was only entitled to VA disability benefits beginning February 28,
    32	2007. The CAVC detailed three components of its analysis. First, Mr. Taylor was not entitled to
    33	relief under the Constitution’s Fifth Amendment Due Process Clause because he did not have a
    34	property interest in his VA benefits prior to February 28, 2007. Relying on Federal Circuit
    35	precedent, the CAVC held that individuals only gain a constitutionally cognizable property interest
    36	in VA benefits upon filing claims for such benefits. Second, the court determined that it lacked
    37	authority to provide Mr. Taylor with equitable relief by ordering VA to establish a process through
    38	which he and similarly situated veterans could establish effective dates for VA Congressional
    39	Research Service 3 benefits preceding their claim-filing dates. Third, the CAVC held that 38 U.S.C.
    40	§ 5110 required the effective date for Mr. Taylor’s VA benefits to be February 28, 2007, the date he
    41	filed his claim. Mr. Taylor appealed the CAVC’s decision to the Federal Circuit. A three-judge
    42	Federal Circuit panel issued its opinion in June 2021, ruling in favor of Mr. Taylor. The court held
    43	the following: (1) “the Veterans Court may exercise such equitable powers, within the scope of its
    44	statutory jurisdiction, to ensure that all veterans entitled to benefits receive them” (that is, the
    45	CAVC had equitable powers beyond those specifically delineated by Congress); (2) the effective date
    46	requirement under 38 U.S.C. § 5110(a)(1) is not jurisdictional and can therefore be subject to
    47	equitable considerations and relief; (3) where “the Government has affirmatively and intentionally
    48	prevented” veterans from seeking medical care and VA benefits to which they are entitled under
    49	threat of criminal prosecution, the CAVC “is within its authority to hold the Government equitably
    50	estopped from asserting that those veterans are not entitled to an earlier effective date”; and (4)
    51	the government is equitably estopped from asserting 38 U.S.C. § 5110(a)(1) against Mr. Taylor
    52	because the government’s actions caused Mr. Taylor to file his benefits claim when he did. The
    53	Federal Circuit reversed the CAVC’s decision and remanded the case. In July 2021, however, the
    54	Federal Circuit voted to hear this case en banc. The full court heard oral argument on February 10,
    55	2022, but weeks later, the U.S. Supreme Court granted review of Arellano v. McDonough, a case
    56	concerning whether 38 U.S.C. § 5110(b)(1), an exception to subsection (a)(1)’s requirements, is
    57	subject to equitable tolling. Section 5110(b)(1) mandates that “[t]he effective date of an award of
    58	disability compensation to a veteran shall be the day following the date of the veteran’s discharge
    59	or release if application therefor is received within one year from such date.” The Federal Circuit
    60	stayed all proceedings in Taylor until the Supreme Court decided Arellano. In January 2023, the
    61	Supreme Court held, in relevant part, that subsection (b)(1) is not subject to equitable tolling
    62	because “[t]he structure of §5110 reinforces Congress’s choice to set effective dates solely as
    63	prescribed in the text,” and because subsection (a)(1) provides “an instruction to attend to
    64	specifically enacted language to the exclusion of general, unenacted carveouts.” Following the
    65	Arellano decision, the Federal Circuit requested supplemental briefing by the parties in light of
    66	the Supreme Court’s holding. Taylor v. McDonough In June 2023, the full Federal Circuit decided in
    67	favor of Mr. Taylor. After finding equitable estoppel unavailable under Section 5110(a)(1) in light
    68	of Supreme Court precedent, the court held that the government violated Mr. Taylor’s constitutional
    69	right to due process under the Fifth Amendment. The court concluded that Mr. Taylor had “a
    70	constitutional right of access to adjudicatory forums” to vindicate his legal entitlements, and that
    71	the VA adjudicatory system and VA benefits are such a forum and entitlement, respectively. The
    72	Federal Circuit further held that the government unconstitutionally denied Mr. Taylor “access to the
    73	adjudication system of VA, the exclusive forum for securing his legal entitlement to the benefits at
    74	issue,” through the secrecy oath and threat of criminal prosecution for violating it. Thus, the
    75	court ruled that the relevant statutory limits on effective dates were “unconstitutional as applied”
    76	in Mr. Taylor’s case. The Federal Circuit determined that Mr. Taylor was entitled to “the effective

76	in Mr. Taylor’s case. The Federal Circuit determined that Mr. Taylor was entitled to “the effective
    77	date he would have had if no unconstitutional denial of access had occurred,” which could be
    78	September 7, 1971, the date Mr. Taylor was discharged, pending VA assessment of this issue on remand
    79	in accordance with the court’s decision. The Federal Circuit summarized its holding’s implications
    80	in the following terms: [W]hen a veteran has been determined to be entitled to benefits for one or
    81	more disabilities connected to participation in the Edgewood program at issue, the required
    82	effective date of such benefits is the date that the veteran would have had in the absence of the
    83	challenged government Congressional Research Service 4 conduct—imposition of the secrecy oath with
    84	no VA route for claim presentation and proof to vindicate the benefits entitlement. The court
    85	reversed the CAVC’s decision and remanded the case. The government has not sought Supreme Court
    86	review as of this writing, though it still has time to do so—petitions must be filed within 90 days
    87	of judgment.

Based on `doc.txt`, the entities that handled Mr. Taylor's disability claim and their responsibilities were as follows:

**VA (Department of Veterans Affairs).** VA received Mr. Taylor's claim for service-connected disability benefits in 2007, and a VA medical examiner diagnosed him with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) resulting from his time at Edgewood, which was reaggravated during his service in Vietnam. VA ultimately granted him a total disability rating with an effective date of February 28, 2007, the day VA received his claim, relying on 38 U.S.C. § 5110 (implemented under 38 C.F.R. § 3.400), which provides that, absent certain exceptions, the effective date shall not be earlier than the date of receipt of the application. After the BVA remanded the case in February 2014, VA procured a secrecy oath that most participants in the Edgewood program signed, and VA and the BVA again concluded that Mr. Taylor was entitled to benefits starting February 28, 2007. The Federal Circuit later held that the government unconstitutionally denied Mr. Taylor access to the VA adjudicatory system—the exclusive forum for securing his legal entitlement to the benefits—through the secrecy oath and threat of criminal prosecution for violating it, and the determination of his effective date (which could be September 7, 1971, the date of his discharge) was left pending VA's assessment of the issue on remand.

**Board of Veterans' Appeals (BVA).** The BVA first reviewed Mr. Taylor's appeal of the VA determination in July 2010, when he sought an effective date of September 7, 1971, the day he was discharged from service. The BVA held that 38 U.S.C. § 5110 prevented the effective date from being any earlier than the day he filed his claim, stating that "there was nothing stopping [Mr. Taylor] from filing the claim . . . earlier and [VA] asking for a delay in the adjudication of the case following the obtaining of important evidence." After the CAVC vacated that decision, the BVA in February 2014 remanded the case to VA to ascertain the secrecy oath's language and reassess the case. In April 2017, the BVA again concluded that benefits began February 28, 2007, giving three reasons: (1) Mr. Taylor could have filed a disability claim earlier than 2007 premised on his experiences serving in Vietnam, which were partially responsible for his PTSD; (2) he could have divulged his participation in the Edgewood program because he had done so on a previous occasion in pursuit of care, though the health care provider at that time did not believe him; and (3) Section 5110 delineates when VA benefits can begin and does not provide for equitable tolling.

**U.S. Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims (CAVC).** In June 2013, a single-judge CAVC decision held that the BVA "failed to provide an adequate statement of reasons or bases for its . . . decision"; the CAVC sought the language of the original secrecy oath, vacated the BVA's decision, and remanded the case. In April 2019, a 2-1 panel of CAVC judges affirmed the BVA's determination that Mr. Taylor was only entitled to benefits beginning February 28, 2007, detailing three components of its analysis: first, Mr. Taylor was not entitled to relief under the Fifth Amendment Due Process Clause because he did not have a property interest in his VA benefits prior to February 28, 2007, relying on Federal Circuit precedent that individuals gain a constitutionally cognizable property interest in VA benefits only upon filing claims; second, the court determined it lacked authority to provide equitable relief by ordering VA to establish a process through which he and similarly situated veterans could establish effective dates preceding their claim-filing dates; and third, the court held that 38 U.S.C. § 5110 required the effective date to be February 28, 2007, the date he filed his claim.

**Federal Circuit.** A three-judge Federal Circuit panel issued its opinion in June 2021, ruling in favor of Mr. Taylor and holding that: (1) the Veterans Court may exercise equitable powers, within the scope of its statutory jurisdiction, to ensure that all veterans entitled to benefits receive them; (2) the effective date requirement under 38 U.S.C. § 5110(a)(1) is not jurisdictional and can be subject to equitable considerations and relief; (3) where the Government has affirmatively and intentionally prevented veterans from seeking medical care and VA benefits to which they are entitled under threat of criminal prosecution, the CAVC is within its authority to hold the Government equitably estopped from asserting that those veterans are not entitled to an earlier effective date; and (4) the government is equitably estopped from asserting § 5110(a)(1) against Mr. Taylor because the government's actions caused him to file his benefits claim when he did. The panel reversed the CAVC's decision and remanded the case. In July 2021, the Federal Circuit voted to hear the case en banc; the full court heard oral argument on February 10, 2022, but then stayed all proceedings in Taylor until the Supreme Court decided Arellano v. McDonough, and after that decision requested supplemental briefing by the parties. In June 2023, the full Federal Circuit decided in favor of Mr. Taylor: after finding equitable estoppel unavailable under Section 5110(a)(1) in light of Supreme Court precedent, the court held that the government violated Mr. Taylor's constitutional right to due process under the Fifth Amendment, concluding that he had "a constitutional right of access to adjudicatory forums" and that the VA adjudicatory system and VA benefits were such a forum and entitlement, and that the government unconstitutionally denied him access through the secrecy oath and threat of criminal prosecution. The court ruled that the relevant statutory limits on effective dates were "unconstitutional as applied" in Mr. Taylor's case, determined that he was entitled to "the effective date he would have had if no unconstitutional denial of access had occurred," which could be September 7, 1971, the date of his discharge, pending VA assessment on remand, and reversed the CAVC's decision and remanded the case.
